Burglary rose compared to Piedmont’s five-year average. Motor vehicle theft, assaults and robberies all declined in 2025. The addition of cameras in Piedmont and neighboring cities has helped officers respond more quickly and coordinate with other departments to address property crime. Burglaries rose compared to Piedmont’s five-year average. Police plan to increase proactive patrols and deploy updated technology to improve response times. “We don’t want to be reactive to crime,” Chief Shavies said. “We want to be proactive, and we want to be out in our community. We want to make it uncomfortable for those who may think of coming into our community and committing crimes.” There was a sharp decline in motor vehicle theft in 2025. articles.text: Piedmont’s new Community Pool opens April 11. From April 11 through April 30, everyone can swim for $5 per visit. This limited-time preview pricing offers a low-cost way to see the new facility, get in the water, and try out the pools before deciding whether a pass is right for you. Starting May 1, visitors can choose between an annual pass, a summer pass, or a drop-in day pass. If you plan to swim more than occasionally, a pool pass is usually the best value. Annual passes are the best deal for regular swimmers and include the most perks for residents, including priority registration for summer swim lessons. Use the pool pass guide to find the option that best fits your household – or visit in-person assistance at the pool at upcoming front-desk help hours: Wednesday, March 11: 1-3 p.m., Thursday, March 12: 4-6 p.m., and Monday, March 16: 4-5 p.m. The Community Pool uses a flexible, “build-a-pass” model. Start with a base pass, Adult, Senior, or Family, then add household members if needed. Youth passes without add-on options are available for teens 14-18 who are the household’s only swimmer. Resident passholders receive additional benefits, including: priority registration for aquatics programs and swim lessons, and extra single-use guest passes. All Piedmont residents receive priority access to summer pass sales and early access to facility rentals. articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont is sponsoring a No Kings 3 rally in Piedmont Park, 711 Highland Ave., Piedmont on Saturday, March 28 from 10:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. This will be one of many hundreds of rallies across the United States. These rallies are expected to draw millions of people who are concerned about the movement away from a society based on democratic principles, the Constitution, and toward an autocratic government headed by a “king” or “queen” who rules the country based on his or her whims. The rally will include brief speeches, songs, and a walk from the park along Highland Avenue. We encourage Piedmonters of all ages and others to come, experience the camaraderie, and, of course, bring your signs! The League of Women Voters of Piedmont is a nonpartisan, grassroots civic organization that encourages informed and active participation in government, works to increase understanding of major public policy issues, and influences public policy through education and advocacy. Membership in the League is open to people 16 years and older, of all gender identities. With over 100 years of experience, the League is one of America’s oldest and most trusted civic nonprofit organizations.

articles.text: The City is extending the deadline for Young Volunteer of the Year nominations to Wednesday, March 18. This year, the City is reviving the Volunteer of the Year award for the first time since 2019. The City is also introducing a new award: Young Volunteer of the Year (under age 25), intended to uplift the meaningful contributions young people make across Piedmont. Piedmont has long been known as the “City of Volunteers.” This award, first introduced in 2014, recognizes community members whose volunteer service helped strengthen Piedmont in 2025 – whether through neighborhood improvement, arts and culture, direct community support, or building a more welcoming and inclusive community. To nominate a volunteer, complete the online nomination form by Wednesday, March 18: https://form.jotform. com/260417487348162. Volunteer service can take many forms – from a long-running commitment to a concentrated effort that made a real difference in a single year. Nominations may recognize service that strengthened Piedmont through areas such as: • Community enrichment: improving neighborhoods and shared spaces, from beautification and clean-ups to public safety and neighborhood initiatives • Culture & Heritage: preserving local history, celebrating Piedmont’s diverse community, and supporting cultural events • Arts: strengthening the community through the visual and performing arts, arts educa- • • tion, events, and mentorship Social: direct community support and humanitarian service, including work with seniors, children, individuals with disabilities, families, and community health and safety Allyship: fostering belonging and solidarity, challenging bias, and helping make Piedmont a safe and welcoming community for everyone Nominations will be reviewed using a blind scoring process that considers measurable impact, service dedication, innovation and leadership, and character and values. Top-scoring nominees are then forwarded to a City Council subcommittee for final selection. Awardees will be recognized at the City’s annual Volunteer Appreciation Reception on April 20, 2026. articles.text: Staff The Bay Area Book Festival (BABF), will return to Berkeley for its 12th year on May 30–31, 2026, under the theme “Writing the Future.” Organizers say the festival will again transform Downtown Berkeley into a multiday celebration of literature, storytelling and cultural activism. This year’s event is expected to feature more than 300 authors and speakers across more than 120 programs on 21 stages, drawing more than 25,000 attendees from across the Bay Area. Festivalgoers will be able to attend 15 free writing workshops, book readings and author conversations, along with opportunities to connect with small presses, emerging writers, book artists and literary organizations. YouthLit, the festival’s youth and family programming track, will expand to two full days this year. Programming will be led by the Oakland-based Social Justice Children’s Book Fair and will include a special activation from ArtEsteem, a West Oakland nonprofit focused on healing arts. Inspired by the legacies of Octavia Butler and James Baldwin, this year’s theme encourages participants to move beyond reacting to crises and toward imaginative action aimed at building more just futures. The festival’s only ticketed events are the headliner conversations, including: A young girl is excited about finding a good book at the festival Headline speaker and writer Rebecca Solnit • World Building, Imagination, and Social Change: Nnedi Okorafor and Marshall Ganz • Write the Future: Publishing Initiatives to Celebrate Diversity: Phoebe Robinson, Kate Gale, Hannah Moushabeck and Cynthia Leitich-Smith • Global Capitalism, Activism, and Hope in Uncertain Times: Saul Williams and Rebecca Solnit • What Haunts Us Still: Surviving and Storytelling: Tananarive Due and Stephen Graham Jones, moderated by Ayize Evertt-Jama • Black Feminist Futurescaping: Alexis Pauline Gumbs and Susana M. articles.text: Awe might seem like a luxury emotion. Something nice to experience on a vacation or in a dramatic moment, but not especially relevant to everyday life. In reality, awe plays a quiet but important role in creativity. When we experience awe, even briefly, our attention expands. We become more curious, more observant, and more open to possibilities we might otherwise overlook. Awe interrupts our routines and reminds us that the world is larger and more interesting than the narrow track our thoughts sometimes run on. When we talk about awe, though, we often imagine something huge. A sweeping landscape. A once in a lifetime trip. A moment so big it stops you in your tracks. Those moments are wonderful when they happen, but they are also rare. If awe depends on something spectacular, most of us will spend a lot of our time waiting for it. Lately I have been wondering if awe might be a little more available than that. Not the cinematic kind, but the quieter version that shows up in ordinary places if we slow down enough to notice it. A leaf that has turned exactly the color of copper. The geometry of frost on a window. The sound of a group of people laughing all at once. The way sunlight moves across a room over the course of an afternoon. The look in a child’s eye when they understand something new. None of these things are dramatic. In fact, most of them happen every day. But they are small reminders that the world is far more intricate and surprising than we usually give it credit for. The problem is not that awe is absent, it’s that we move through our days so quickly that we miss it. So here is a small experiment to try. For the next week, choose one ordinary moment each day and look at it a little longer than usual. Maybe it is something outside your window. Maybe it is a pattern, a sound, or a moment of interaction between people that grabs your attention. Stay with it for thirty seconds or a minute and see what you notice once your attention settles. You do not have to photograph it, analyze it, or turn it into anything. The key is just to notice it. Creativity often begins with this kind of attention. Before we make something new, we have to remember that the world itself is already full of interesting things. Awe does not always arrive as a thunderbolt. Sometimes it begins as a quiet realization that there is more here than we first saw. Nina Meehan is a keynote speaker, workshop facilitator and coach with a specialization in creativity and communication. https://ninameehan.com/
articles.title: Thinking Outside the Classroom Creativity experiment: Practicing awe at human scale

Thinking Outside the Classroom Creativity experiment: Practicing awe at human scale By Nina Meehan Awe might seem like a luxury emotion. Something nice to experience on a vacation or in a dramatic moment, but not especially relevant to everyday life. In reality, awe plays a quiet but important role in creativity. When we experience awe, even briefly, our attention expands. We become more curious, more observant, and more open to possibilities we might otherwise overlook. Awe interrupts our routines and reminds us that the world is larger and more interesting than the narrow track our thoughts sometimes run on. When we talk about awe, though, we often imagine something huge. A sweeping landscape. A once in a lifetime trip. A moment so big it stops you in your tracks. Those moments are wonderful when they happen, but they are also rare. If awe depends on something spectacular, most of us will spend a lot of our time waiting for it. Lately I have been wondering if awe might be a little more available than that. Not the cinematic kind, but the quieter version that shows up in ordinary places if we slow down enough to notice it. A leaf that has turned exactly the color of copper. The geometry of frost on a window. The sound of a group of people laughing all at once. The way sunlight moves across a room over the course of an afternoon. The look in a child’s eye when they understand something new. None of these things are dramatic. In fact, most of them happen every day. But they are small reminders that the world is far more intricate and surprising than we usually give it credit for. The problem is not that awe is absent, it’s that we move through our days so quickly that we miss it. So here is a small experiment to try. For the next week, choose one ordinary moment each day and look at it a little longer than usual. Maybe it is something outside your window. Maybe it is a pattern, a sound, or a moment of interaction between people that grabs your attention. Stay with it for thirty seconds or a minute and see what you notice once your attention settles. You do not have to photograph it, analyze it, or turn it into anything. The key is just to notice it. Creativity often begins with this kind of attention. Before we make something new, we have to remember that the world itself is already full of interesting things. Awe does not always arrive as a thunderbolt. Sometimes it begins as a quiet realization that there is more here than we first saw. articles.text: Debate duo preps for NPDL National Parliamentary Debate League TOC in San Diego Piedmont High School’s Joey Assalian and Noah Sarlin turned in impressive performances in the 2026 Evergreen Invitational Parliamentary Debate Tournament last month finishing second. The team advanced through the competitive open division field in the online tournament before falling just short of the championship in a hard-fought final. Parliamentary debate is a fast-paced, two-on-two format modeled on the traditions of the British Parliament. Teams receive their motion, a resolution on a political, philosophical, or social issue, just minutes before the round begins, with no notes or prepared evidence allowed. The pair went 4-1 in preliminary rounds to earn a high seed heading into the elimination rounds, then rattled off three consecutive wins to punch their ticket to the championship round. There, they faced Nueva School’s Asudani & Bernhard, who ultimately claimed the title, in a finals that went Nueva’s way. Debaters must construct and deliver compelling arguments entirely on their feet, alternating speeches between the Government side, which defends the motion, and the Opposition side, which challenges it. Points of Information — brief interjections where opponents challenge a speaker mid-speech — add an extra layer of strategy to every exchange. A runner-up finish at the online invitational represents a significant milestone for the Piedmont duo, who have shown steady improvement throughout the season. Piedmont coach Holden Carrillo expressed pride in his debaters’ trajectory. “Joey and Noah have put in the work, and performances like this are a reflection of that,” Carrillo said. “Reaching the finals of a tournament this competitive tells you a lot about where they are as a team. The goal now is to take everything we learned here and be ready when it counts most.” “Getting to a final is great, but what excites me is how they’re thinking on their feet now — the speed of their analysis, the way they’re adapting mid-round,” said fellow Piedmont coach Will White. “That’s exactly the kind of debating that wins at a TOC.” Assalian and Sarlin will compete next at the NPDL Tournament of Champions, held April 10-12 at Canyon Crest Academy in San Diego. Described as the culminating celebration of high school parliamentary debate in the United States, the NPDLTOC draws qualifiers who have earned bids through sanctioned tournaments or at-large selection. articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District will continue to accept nominations for the 2026 Arthur Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award until March 13. The award is presented annually to individuals who have volunteered their efforts over a period of time and made a difference because of their involvement and commitment to Piedmont’s youth. Previous recipients include: Hunter McCreary (1998); Ann Chandler (1999); Ruth Cuming (2000); Lisa Lomenzo (2001); jointly by Cathie Geddeis and Marion Souyoultzis (2002); jointly by Fritz and Mary Wooster (2003); Elizabeth (Betsy) Gentry (2004); Cynthia Gorman (2005); Grier Graff (2006); Julia Burke (2007); Maude Pervere (2008); jointly to Anne-Marie Lamarche and Mark Menke (2009); Janiele Maffei Tovani (2010); Andrea Swenson (2011), June Monach (2012), Bill Drum (posthumously) and Mary Ireland (2013), Ray Perman (2014), Jennifer Fox (2015), Katie Korotzer (2016), Hilary Cooper (2017) Holly Hanke (2018), Cathy Glazier (2019), Sue Smegal (2020), Ken Li (2021), Eileen Ruby (2022), David Ragones (2023), Sarah Pearson (2024) and most recently, Cory Smegal in 2025. Art Hecht was a tireless community volunteer who was dedicated to students in both Piedmont and Oakland. He served on Piedmont’s Board of Education from 1970 to 1982. Art also was very active with the Piedmont Continuation High School (now called Millennium High School). In 1998, the Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award was established in his memory by School Board member Dewey Watson. Nominations for this award are now being sought and will be kept strictly confidential. The deadline for nominations is March 13. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, who will be recognized at the May 6, Board of Education meeting, where the honoree’s good works will be acknowledged. Nomination forms are available on the bottom of the Superintendent’s webpage Piedmont. k12.ca.us/ref/superintendent, in the District Office (760 Magnolia Avenue), or by calling Rosalina Barrios, Executive Assistant to the Superintendent, at 594-2614. Rotarians also participated and assisted in the fundraising for the “Corre por Amor” or Run for Love, a 5K-12K race on March 16, 2025 that supported individuals with spina bifida and other disabilities. Rotarians and supporters of the race walked while many of the patients pushed their way in wheelchairs. The Rotary Group visited Fundacion Monica Uribe por Amor which also supports individuals with spina bifida, and spent time with patients to play ping pong, and have wheelchair races. “We had wheelchair races with the kids. I’ll give you one guess who won the races, and it wasn’t the rotarians,” Bruck said with a smile. Rotarians also visited the aquaponics project at Fundacion Hogar San Jose, where fish provide nutrients to grow vegetables. Rotarian funded projects brought clean water to rural schools by buying water filters, chlorination equipment, and renovating bathrooms for eights schools. Their efforts buoyed the support of both local Colombia and other international clubs to create water wells, tanks, and pumps for clean water, benefiting 7,500 indigenous residents in rural areas. “When you become a [Rotary] member, you get a little rotary pin with the rotary wheel. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team’s season came to an end on Thursday, March 5, in a 51-49 loss to No. 6 seed Central East of Fresno in the second round of the Division 1 CIF State tournament at Binks Rawlings Gym. Piedmont was the No. 3 seed. The team opened with a 63-57 win over No. 14 Antelope on Tuesday, March 3. “We knew Central East would be a tough team, obviously everyone at this stage is,” said PHS coach Bryan Gardere. “We had some costly turnovers, but collectively I thought we did a good job. We just ran out of time.” PHS opened strongly with a 19-4 lead by the end of the first period, but the Bengals stormed back to take a 28-22 by halftime. With an aggressive press, CEHS went on a 19-1 run to take a 23-22 lead with 1:17 left, and added five more points. “We got off to a good start, but the second quarter was obviously the difference in the game. I still think if you take a few mistakes away, we’re right there,” Gardere reflected. Trailing 51-41 with 2:11 left in the game, the Highlanders didn’t quit, going on an eight-point run to the final buzzer. It was a dramatic final seconds of the game, where Jenelle Solis stole a ball that led to a layup by Nia Jackson bouncing off the rim multiple times, leading to an offensive rebound by Andrea Martin. “Although it was a hard loss, we’re still staying together. We’re going to go into the offseason really working hard. When we get to this stage next year, we know what to do,” Martin said. Despite falling short, the Highlanders’ future is still bright. Martin, Solis, Savannah Dennig, and Jaden Jones will be juniors next season, Alexa Ba will be a sophomore, and Taylor White and Jackson are poised to be the only senior of the bunch. Saniyah Johnson is the only graduating senior on the team. “I’m really proud of our seniors. I’m just happy we got to play together. We’re losing one senior, but hey, it’s time for everyone to step up and get better,” Martin said. “We’re definitely going to use this as fuel. We only lose Saniyah, who is a big player to lose, but we still have a good core Staff Photos Piedmont’s season came to an end against Central East in the second round of the D1 CIF State tournament. coming back. We’ll take this loss, learn from it, and take it into next season,” mentioned Ba. 51-49 loss to Central East Piedmont came out hot with a 19-4 lead in the first quarter, including 11 points from Martin and eight from Ba. But Central East was on fire in the second quarter, scoring 24 points, including four 3-pointers. In the third quarter, both teams traded baskets until the Bengals went on a 9-2 run to build a 10-point lead at 41-31 with two minutes remaining. After that Jaden Jones hit a 3-pointer, while Martin hit a pair of free throws and White converted a layup to end the quarter in a 43-38 deficit. Solis made a 3-pointer early in the second, but Central East followed with eight straight points to extend its lead to 51-41 with 2:11 left in the game. From there, PHS scored its eight remaining points to finish the game. Martin hit a layup, then Solis assisted Johnson, while Martin stole a ball, turning it to Solis for an assist to Ba with 1:06 left—51-47. After back and forth trades of possession, White stole a ball, leading to a bucket by Martin with 29 seconds left, putting PHS within one possession at 51-49. Central East gained possession, leading to a steal by Solis. Nia Jackson went up for a layup, and the ball dramatically bounced off the rim before falling away. Martin grabbed an offensive rebound with 14 seconds left, leading to a timeout. Then, on Piedmont’s ensuing inbounds play, Martin went up hoping for a pass on the mark, but it was slightly behind her, leading to a turnover with 10.5 seconds left. CEHS was able to kill the clock from there. articles.text: Staff Photos Massimo Mittone hit a grand slam home run in Piedmont’s 4-2 win over Head-Royce. Piedmont High’s baseball team remains undefeated through its first three games of the season. They beat Head-Royce 4-2 at Humphries Diamond on Wednesday, March 4 and wound up tying Cal High 3-3 on Friday, March 6. The game was tied in the ninth inning after the sun set. The Highlanders came back from early deficits in both games. They trailed 2-0 to Cal High before scoring three runs in the bottom of the third, and trailed 2-0 to Head-Royce before Massimo Mittone smacked a grand slam in the same inning. “Mo is a big player for us on the mound and with the bat,” coach Eric Olson said. Piedmont was able to lean on its defense in both games. They had a double play against the Jayhawks and forced 13 ground outs against California. “I don’t know if there’s a better defensive infield in the East Bay. We really want our pitchers to pitch for contact and we’ll catch the ball for him,” Olson said. The pair of results brings Piedmont’s record to 2-0-1 (W-LT) to start its season. 3-3 tie with California Cal High led 2-0 after the top of the second inning, while Piedmont pulled one back in the bottom half. The Highlanders went ahead 3-2 in the bottom of the third, while California scored the tying run in top of the seventh. Neither team scored in the eighth inning, leading to a conclusion of play with a lack of sunlight. In the bottom second, Jack Meyjes led off with a walk, while freshman Ben Sorensen drew a one-out walk. Sophomore outfielder Aiden Bell then cracked a single to move Meyjes to load the bases. Enzo Ong grounded into a fielder’s choice to bring in Meyjes from third, but that was all the Highlanders could muster. Piedmont pulled ahead in the bottom of the third after Lucas Delventhal led off with a single, while Diego Delventhal drew a walk. Jonah Cha-Foster kept it going with a single to load the bases, once again. That’s when Jack Meyjes slugged a single to center field to tie up the game 2-2. Massimo Mittone hit a sacrifice fly to score Diego Delventhal, while Cal High was able to end the inning by throwing out Jonah Cha-Foster had two hits against Cal High, and one hit against Head-Royce to go along with a run and stolen base. Aiden Bell went 1-for-3 with a double against Head-Royce, and 1-for-2 against Cal High.

articles.text: Tennis is back at the Corey Reich Tennis Center, as the Piedmont High boys’ tennis team opened its season with a 4-2 record. The Highlanders lost 9-0 at Acalanes on Thursday, February 26, swept Arroyo 7-0 in San Lorenzo on Thursday, March 5, while they went 3-1 at the James Logan Tournament in Union City on Friday and Saturday, March 6-7. At the tournament, Piedmont claimed 4-3 wins over three schools, including Granada, Emerald, and Heritage. They closed with a 5-2 loss to Campolindo. “We’re off to a good start. We played Friday and Saturday, and did well even without our top player, Lucas Smolko. We took second and lost in the finals to Campolindo,” coach Jim Landes said. Smolko leads the singles lineup for the final year of his high school career. He’ll be the Western Alameda County Conference favorite to win his third consecutive league singles title, while he’s seeking his first North Coast Section title after reaching the finals in 2023 and 2025. Should he reach the NCS individual tournament singles’ title match, he’ll likely face HeadRoyce’s Dylan Donovan. Smolko lost to Donovan in three sets, 5-7, 6-1, 6-3, in last year’s final. “It’s possible for Lucas to take that next step, but he’s got Dylan to contend with again. I’m sure it’ll be another close battle between them,” Landes said. Behind Smolko is fellow fouryear starter, Nate Welch. Freshman Ari Moskovitz has emerged as Landes’ No. 3 singles starter, and sophomore Emilio Misra enters his second year on the squad at No. 4. “Nate is our No. 2, He’s starting to play pretty well. articles.text: The international photography exhibition Ocean Photographer of the Year will make its United States debut April 24 inside a historic World War II aircraft hangar at Alameda Point. The exhibition, presented by Oceanographic Magazine and Blancpain, will run for one month and feature a selection of winning and finalist images from the global Ocean Photographer of the Year competition. The show is hosted locally by West End Arts District in partnership with Bay Photo Lab. Now in its fifth year, the competition received more than 15,000 submissions from photographers worldwide. The exhibition includes images from categories such as wildlife, fine art, adventure, conservation, human connection, and young photographer of the year, along with the Female Fifty Fathoms Award recognizing women in ocean photography. “We’re thrilled to bring Ocean Photographer of the Year to Alameda Point and to invite the community to experience this powerful ode to the ocean in such a unique setting,” Tara Pilbrow, executive director of West End Arts District, said in a press release. “By breathing new life into Alameda Point’s military history, we’re also expressing our commitment to the kind of future we want to see: one rooted in creativity, environmental awareness, and shared cultural experiences.” Alongside the international exhibition, visitors can explore “Bay Perspectives,” a gallery featuring ocean photography focused on the San Francisco Bay and the California coast. The space will also include interactive marine science exhibits presented by the Sailing Science Center. “The stories behind these photographs are as compelling as the visuals themselves – they challenge us to see the ocean not just as a place of wonder, but as a world in need of our care,” said Daryl Karp, director and chief executive officer of the Australian National Maritime Museum. Public hours will run Saturdays and Sundays from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., with additional programs scheduled on Thursdays and Fridays. An opening gala hosted by Bay Photo Lab will also mark the company’s 50th anniversary. “Our mission is to share the ocean with non-ocean goers and photography is the most awesome conduit to do that,” said Will Harrison of Oceanographic Magazine. “Underwater photography is one of the most powerful allies in our fight to preserve and protect the ocean,” added Gaël Nicolle of Blancpain. For more information and to purchase tickets to the exhibition and events, visit www.westendartsdistrict.org.
articles.title: Ocean Photographer of the Year exhibition debuts at Alameda Point April 24

The Oakland Museum of California’s (OMCA) free community-gathering evening event series “Friday Nights” returns next month, kicking off the spring season with live performances and weekly food concessions. OMCA hosts free, family-friendly community events every Friday at 5 p.m. throughout spring and summer, featuring live music, immersive arts activities and late-night museum access with the purchase of a museum ticket. Bring a blanket and lawn chairs to relax on the museum’s large lawn, where live music and entertainment takes place throughout the evening. Guests can bring their own food and refreshments or purchase from a stationed food truck on-site. A rotating list of vendors will be parked on 10th Street between Oak and Fallon Streets adjacent to the museum. No outside alcohol is permitted. Friday Night events are always free and open to the public, but late-night museum access requires a ticket purchase. Visit https://museumca.org/about-friday-nights-at-omca-with-off-thegrid/ to learn more.

articles.text: Opera San Jose performs March 17 - 19 Spring blooms are beginning to appear at Filoli, where tens of thousands of tulips, daffodils and hyacinths are coming into season. The historic estate features more than 16 acres of formal gardens and a collection of native and exotic plants. In March, orchids, magnolias and citrus blossoms begin to open across the property. Visitors may also see tulips, irises, wisteria, peonies and seasonal wildflowers. Spring is considered the estate’s signature season. Gardeners plant more than 130,000 bulbs each year, filling garden beds and containers throughout the grounds. Opera San Jose will present a preview of its 2026–27 season at Filoli with selections from La Traviata. Performances are scheduled March 17–19 in the estate’s ballroom. Evening performances begin at 7 p.m., with tickets priced from $75 to $105. Guests may also purchase champagne for an additional fee. Filoli is open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Evening tickets allow visitors to tour the house and gardens beginning at 5 p.m. and remain on the grounds until closing at 8 p.m. Evening tickets are released weekly for the following four weeks. Food and drinks are available on-site at the Quail Cafe and the Vegetable Garden Bar. More information is available at Filoli’s website at https://filoli. org/ or by calling (650) 364-8300. pages.text: 16 16 Wednesday, March 11, 2026 Arts & Entertainment Ocean Photographer of the Year exhibition debuts at “Friday Nights” returns to Oakland Museum of California next month Alameda Point April 24 By Allyson Aleksey The international photography exhibition Ocean Photographer of the Year will make its United States debut April 24 inside a historic World War II aircraft hangar at Alameda Point. The exhibition, presented by Oceanographic Magazine and Blancpain, will run for one month and feature a selection of winning and finalist images from the global Ocean Photographer of the Year competition. The show is hosted locally by West End Arts District in partnership with Bay Photo Lab. Now in its fifth year, the competition received more than 15,000 submissions from photographers worldwide. The exhibition includes images from categories such as wildlife, fine art, adventure, conservation, human connection, and young photographer of the year, along with the Female Fifty Fathoms Award recognizing women in ocean photography. “We’re thrilled to bring Ocean Photographer of the Year to Alameda Point and to invite the community to experience this powerful ode to the ocean in such a unique setting,” Tara Pilbrow, executive director of West End Arts District, said in a press release. “By breathing new life into Alameda Point’s military history, we’re also expressing our commitment to the kind of future we want to see: one rooted in creativity, environmental awareness, and shared cultural experiences.” Alongside the international exhibition, visitors can explore “Bay Perspectives,” a gallery featuring ocean photography focused on the San Francisco Bay and the California coast. The space will also include interactive marine science exhibits presented by the Sailing Science Center. “The stories behind these photographs are as compelling as the visuals themselves – they challenge us to see the ocean not just as a place of wonder, but as a world in need of our care,” said Daryl Karp, director and chief executive officer of the Australian National Maritime Museum. Public hours will run Saturdays and Sundays from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., with additional programs scheduled on Thursdays and Fridays. An opening gala hosted by Bay Photo Lab will also mark the company’s 50th anniversary. “Our mission is to share the ocean with non-ocean goers and photography is the most awesome conduit to do that,” said Will Harrison of Oceanographic Magazine. “Underwater photography is one of the most powerful allies in our fight to preserve and protect the ocean,” added Gaël Nicolle of Blancpain. For more information and to purchase tickets to the exhibition and events, visit www.westendartsdistrict.org. articles.text: A previous year’s performance of Don Quixote. San Francisco Ballet will present Don Quixote, inspired by the novel of the same name by Miguel de Cervantes, at the War Memorial Opera House from March 19 - 29. The production is based on the 19th-century choreography of Marius Petipa and Alexander Gorsky and was restaged for the company in 2003 by former artistic director Helgi Tomasson and choreographer Yuri Possokhov. The ballet features music by Ludwig Minkus. The story follows the romance between Kitri and Basilio and is known for technically demanding choreography, including the Act III pas de deux and a jump associated with the character of Kitri. The production includes 152 roles performed across four casts. Principal dancers scheduled to perform Kitri include Sasha De Sola, Nikisha Fogo, Wona Park and Madeline Woo, along with first soloist Katherine Barkman. Dancers performing Basilio include principals Cavan Conley, Gabriele Francesco Frola, Esteban Hernández and Wei Wang, and first soloist Joshua Jack Price. Scenic and costume design is by Martin Pakledinaz. Lighting design is by James F. Ingalls. Evening performances will include lobby performances by Theatre Flamenco of San Francisco featuring dancer Carola Zertuche, guitarist Jesse Torres and singer Clara Rodriguez. Photo courtesy of San Francisco Ballet Opening night activities will take place after the performance, while other evening activations will begin about 30 minutes before curtain. The ballet runs about 2 hours and 34 minutes, including two intermissions. Pre-performance talks with company artists are scheduled for March 20, March 22, March 27 and March 29 at the opera house. A performance ticket is required to attend. Tickets are available through the company’s ticket services and website. Casting and ticket prices are subject to change. Don Quixote is a family-friendly ballet experience for all ages. Visit www.sfballet.org to purchase tickets.

articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse recently announced that it is extending the Tony Award-winning musical Once, playing onstage now through March 29. Featuring a book by Enda Walsh and music and lyrics by Glen Hansard and Markéta Irglová, Once is based on the 2007 film that earned the Academy Award for Best Original Song for “Falling Slowly.” Set in Dublin, the story follows an Irish busker and a Czech immigrant who form a deep connection through music during a life-changing week of songwriting and collaboration. The production is directed by Josh Marx, with music direction by Michael Patrick Wiles and choreography by Erin Rose Solorio. Actors perform their own instruments onstage, creating a pub-style atmosphere that underscores the show’s themes of community and artistic partnership. “I’ve always loved Once because it digs into something I think about a lot: what music really is and how it connects us as human beings,” Marx said. “I loved the movie Once when I first saw it — and then the Broadway production pulled me in even deeper, especially the way it evoked a sense of community; similar to drinking a pint of Guinness in an Irish pub while patrons play music together. For Berkeley Playhouse’s production, we’re looking to put something truly special together; each actor plays their own instrument (sometimes more than one!), and we want to create an unforgettable experience that capitalizes on the amazing talent that we’re bringing into the room.” Jake Gale and Gillian Eichenberger lead the cast as Guy and Girl. For tickets or more information, call (510) 845-8542 x351 or visit berkeleyplayhouse.org. Photo by Ben Krantz Jake Gale and Gillian Eichenberger perform in Berkeley Playhouse’s production of Once. articles.text: Sentimental Value, written and directed by Joachim Trier, who is well known for his cinematic exploration of family relationships (The Worst Person in the World). The film has received nine Oscar nominations to include Best Picture, Best Actress, Best Director, Best Supporting Actor, and Best Supporting Actress (both Elle Fanning and Inga Ibsdolder Lilleass). The story focuses on the fractured relationships between renowned Norwegian film director Gustav Borg (Stellan Skarsgard) and his daughters Nora (Renate Reinsve) and Agnes (Inga Ibsdolter Lilleaas). Central to their backstory is the choice Gustav made early in their lives to use his divorce from his wife, Sissel, as a reason to leave Norway and pursue a career writing and directing. That impactful decision has caused years of estrangement from his daughters. Unexpectedly their mother dies, and Gustav returns to Oslo where he awkwardly attempts to reconnect with Nora and Agnes who now have separate lives. Nora is a fragile stage actress and Agnes is married with a son. Gustav meets with Nora and inelegantly tells her he has written a script about his mother, Karin, and would like her to portray her grandmother. It is set during WWII, and will be filmed in their multigenerational family home where the sisters grew up. Karin was captured by the Nazis, charged with belonging to the Norwegian resistance, and tortured, something she refused to talk about after the war. Agnes, who is an historian, discovers, later in the film, the trauma her grandmother endured. When Gustav was seven, Karin committed suicide. Nora, absent any real discussion with Gustav about the script or about her deep resentment due to his long absence from their lives, refuses the part and abruptly leaves. In her wake, the distance tween the two remains Stellan Skarsgård and Elle Fanning in Sentimental Value unresolved, and seems to come as a surprise to Gustav. Without the detachment of the camera lens, and his inherent Nordic reserve, he seems incapable of engaging with either Nora or Agnes. The first two acts of Sentimental Value almost feel like a prologue to what follows. Gustav finds an American actress, Rachel Kemp (Elle Fanning), who does not speak Norwegian agrees to take the role, yet soon begins to feel that the essence of Karin is ever elusive. I experienced the abrupt cuts from scene to scene puzzling. Was it the absence of connecting exposition? The film is character-driven, yet I found myself having to work to understand certain scenes. For example, the film cuts to Nora, in bed with, I assumed, a fellow actor. But this relationship is unexplained and quickly dropped. And there’s vagueness or continuing distance that are never resolved between the daughters and their father. And yet, there is a scene with Rachel who is comforted by Gustav when she sadly explains she cannot continue in her portrayal of Karin. There were also moments when I realized I had left the story, which is a red flag, a signal perhaps, that though I wanted to care about and understand these people and their nuanced history, I often felt lost. But clearly, Sentimental Value has been praised by the voting Academy, as have the actors. Sentimental Value. Norwegian film with subtitles. Written and directed by Joachim Trier. Starring Stellan Skarsgard, Renate Reinsve, Elle Fanning and Ilse Ibsdotler. Rated R. 2hrs 13mi. Released 2025. Streaming on Prime/Fandango/Apple tv

Join us for “Music … For Awhile” with selections from Dowling, Purcell, Schubert, Schumann, and Copland. This award-winning young but seasoned duo has performed extensively throughout Europe and Asia. Meet the Duo at a complimentary reception following the performance. Admission is $20 at the door, and donations to help with travel costs will be appreciated. The program, called Resonant Offering, will be a rare and dazzling exploration into a musical tradition as old as or older than our Western Classical traditions, with this very high-level trio of expert musicians with decades of experience in the genre. Buy advance tickets at https://events.com/r/tickets/1030338, or pay at the door for $5 more. Sunday, March 15, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Jazz & Pop Piano Trio Bill Jackman, Albert Brooks, and Marshall Perry bring you an assortment of traditional Irish music and songs celebrating the spirit of St. Patrick’s Day, in the intimate comfort of our Classic Jazz Club, with table seating and refreshments included. Buy your advance tickets at https://events.com/r/tickets/1021877. Saturday, March 21, 6:00 p.m. Yun Janice Lu Solo Piano Recital Taiwanese pianist Yun Janice Lu is recognized as one of the most compelling artists of her generation. She believes music is the strongest medium for storytelling, a conviction that leads her to build creative and cohesive performance programs. She aims to offer audiences a vast variety of repertoire, contributing to a colorful and engaging listening experience. Currently a Doctor of Musical Arts (DMA) candidate at the New England Music Conservatory, Janice already holds two Masters degrees from the Yale School of Music. She made her orchestral debut with the Taiwan Youth Orchestra at age 14. Janice has won many major international awards and has played worldwide. Her program, Shadow & Radiance explores contrasts of color and darkness, fire, and hope with the music of J.S. Bach, Scarlatti, Janáček, Hamelin, William Bolcom, Scriabin, and Robert Schumann. Advance tickets are available at https://events.com/r/tickets/1031111. Sunday, March 22, 4:00 p.m. Berkeley Symphony & Friends Chamber Concert Join Dianne Nicolini, the voice of Classical California, for an afternoon of her favorite French music, called French Connections. This concert leads listeners into the beauty of a spring morning imagined by Lili Boulanger in Poulenc’s lyrical sonata for flute, Debussy’s vision of Cythera, a meditation from Massenet’s opera Thais, and Ravel’s most ambitious chamber work, the Piano Trio. Dianne Nicolini was the first female full-time announcer on KXTR in Kansas City, on KKHI in San Francisco, and on Classical California. She was inducted into the Bay Area Radio Hall of Fame in 2016. She has kept midday listeners company on Classical California since 1994. For advance tickets go to https://purchase.berkeleysymphony.org/Events or call the Box Office at (510) 841-2800. articles.text: Opera was the most popular form of entertainment for a very long time. Usually in opera lots of people get killed. So many in fact that opera could have been a morticians’ desideratum. Curiously, in Mozart’s marvelous opera Cosi fan tutte no one dies. This is very surprising. And the opera is a comedy nonetheless. Mozart was ingenious. The plot of the opera is ridiculous. That’s the way opera stories are. In some ways Mark Twain could have been one of the inspirations. Cosi fan tutte has many of the characteristics of Mark Twain plot and it is centered around the social mores of men and women. Perhaps I should say “men versus women.” That alone makes it both ridiculous and realistic. Mozart took these things into account and produced an extremely melodious opera. One beautiful aria is followed by other beautiful arias, one after another. The recent production by the Livermore Valley opera company was memorable. The small orchestra began with an energetic overture. In general the musicians were very polished. Conductor Alexandra Katzman led a very spirited performance. The curtain rose, and the singers took command of the story. The cast was evenly divided featuring three women, notably Meryl Dominguez, Courtney Miller, and Megan Potter and male leads Sid Chand, Samuel Kid and Eugene Brancoveanu. Erie Mills deserves credit for her general direction as do Bruce Olstad and Robert Harriot. This opera is popular for good reason. The audience is encouraged to consider many possibilities of social mores. Despite the turmoil, everything ends happily. Shakespeare would have summed it up by saying “all’s well that ends well.” Have a look at the schedule for the next series of operas presented by the Livermore Valley opera Company. You’ll be happy you did. Sunday in Piedmont An outstanding cello and piano recital was presented Sunday evening in the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Miles Reed is an outstanding young cellist and a laureate of the most recent Klein International Competition. For this program, he was joined by the acclaimed pianist Amy Zanrosso. Their program was notable for its diversity and high spirits. A song without words by Mendelssohn began the program. What followed was a miniature suite for unaccompanied cello composed by Paul Wiancko which Miles Reed introduced Mozart’s opera Cosi fan tutte as presented by the Livermore Valley Opera Company was as proficient as it was colorful.

articles.text: A smooth collie stands stacked in the ring, ready for Best in Show Judging. Many dog owners wonder at some point whether their furry friend has what it takes to strut their stuff at a show. The purebred dog show world is a very unique one which demands not only a very healthy animal, but specific training designed to demonstrate to a judge that your dog is the ideal version of its breed. Hence, mixed breed dogs cannot compete.The breed standard is a written description of a perfect canine individual, typically mentioning the desirable body structure, coat, and gait. It may also include things like temperament or a specific facial expression desired for the breed. Show dogs are compared to this breed standard in the ring. Whether you decide to show your own dog or not, attending an all-breed AKC show is a great way to start off your dog show education. Handlers and breeders alike are typically happy to explain what is happening in the ring as well as what the judge is looking for in their specific breed. When attending your first show, make sure that you always ask permission before petting any dogs and avoid carrying around food as it may distract dogs. Take some time to watch your preferred breed in the ring. You’ll notice that they typically start with the youngest dogs and move upwards in maturity. It is well worth it to stay until the end when the first place dogs from all seven groups compete for Best in Show. Interestingly, these dogs are not being compared to each other, but rather against their individual breed standards. Needless to say, a judge must have a great deal of knowledge to make this decision! Curious about showing your own dog? A great way to test the waters is to enter your puppy in the beginner puppy competition (B-Pup). This is a low stakes show where puppies get to practice. This may give you an idea of whether your dog has a show career in their future based on how they place. Before committing to a show career, consider a couple pros and cons of the conformation show life. Shows may take up many of your weekends and require significant funding for travel and supplies. Additionally, your dog must remain intact (not neutered or spayed) in order to participate in breed shows. For many owners, this is a dealbreaker, as hormone-driven behaviors can quickly get out of hand and lead to lifelong behavioral problems. When making this decision, consider your individual lifestyle and, after attending a few shows, whether you feel this is truly a passion for you. Above all, dog shows should be joyful for both you and your canine companion! Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. To contact her, please call 510–507– 2017, email Sierra109@gmail. com, or visit her website at www. oakhillsdogtraining.weebly.com.

articles.text: On Monday, March 2, the First Mondays Reading Group drew an excellent turnout of 21 participants for its monthly discussion at Piedmont Community Hall. The group met to discuss their March selection, Harlem Shuffle by Colson Whitehead. A two-time Pulitzer Prize winner for The Underground Railroad (2017) and The Nickel Boys (2020). This is his 2021 novel that takes place in Harlem between 1959 and 1964. It is a crime fiction, a family saga, a morality play, a social novel about race and power, and is also an homage to Harlem. Whitehead’s Ray Carney lives in Harlem with his wife, with whom he is expecting their second child. Although Ray comes from a family with a criminal history, he makes his living working as an upstanding furniture store owner and salesman. Ray has steered his life toward an honest living, but his cousin Freddie is descending into Harlem’s criminal underworld. But money is tight for Ray, especially with his sales of sofas on installment plans, so when Freddie occasionally drops off a ring or necklace, Ray doesn’t ask where they came from, and he knows a jeweler downtown who doesn’t ask questions either. Freddie sets up a robbery and volunteers Ray to fence the stolen goods, but the heist goes wrong. This sends a cast of criminals into Ray’s life and forces him into a personal struggle between doing what is right/legal and getting ahead. The novel is divided into three parts and covers three separate capers that are set in 1959, 1961, and 1964, and ends with the Harlem riot of 1964. Harlem Shuffle was almost universally well-received by the readers. It was an easy, fast, and fun read. The readers felt like they were really in NYC and unfortunately, strongly influences the world. The flavor of Harlem and New York City at the time was one that the readers could relate to. Some reflected on their own 1960s NYC experiences and also considered what Harlem is today. It may have changed some, but its energy and demographics are still vibrant, diverse, and a little scary. While some readers felt Whitehead’s characterizations were rich, others wished he had developed supporting characters, like Ray’s wife. And there were a few readers who were not at all enamored with the book. They could not get invested in the characters and were disappointed with the subject matter. Additionally, the action seemed repetitive. The book may be a good social novel, as well as a crime, relationship story, but there was not enough in the book to capture their emotions and hold their interest. Readers were interested in reading more about Ray and Freddie in Whitehead’s trilogy and reading his other award-winning novels, but everyone seemed interested in having more First Mondays Reading Group discussions like this one. The group has selected Secondhand Time: The Last of the Soviets, a 2013 book by Belarusian Nobel laureate Svetlana Alexievich, for its April book and The God of the Woods by Liz Moore for May. The readers chose Barbarian Days: A Surfing Life by William Finnegan for their June read. With all their business done, they took a group photo at the back of the Community Hall. The readers will meet at the Community Hall for their next discussion on April 6 at 1:30 p.m. New readers are welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required at https://bit. ly/3R86PP4. Harlem Shuffle by Colson Whitehead marveled at Whitehead’s writing skills. He is a highly accomplished wordsmith and thinks in ways that most people cannot imagine. His language is vivid, and he can bring his thoughts to the page in rich and captivating prose. The readers got the idea and understood why Whitehead was awarded a MacArthur Fellowship (genius grant) in 2002 at the age of 32. Whitehead vividly paints the picture of New York City in the 1960s. It is a vibrant, dynamic place with an elite set of upperclass African Americans, but also more common people, like Ray and Freddie, who are just trying to survive. The group could understand how a guy like Ray could become a “little bent” while trying not to be a crook. The 1960s in Harlem were tough. The group could imagine themselves in Ray’s situation, being presented with shady dealings and rationalizing behaviors that were a slippery slope into criminality. The group felt this was not just a Harlem thing. It was and still is everywhere. articles.text: Forty-five walkers and four K-9 companions gathered at the Exedra last Wednesday morning for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays outing. The group set out to revisit several of Piedmont’s parks and take a closer look at some of the city’s Heritage Trees. The Piedmont Heritage Tree Program was created in 2018 by the City Council based on a recommendation from the Park Commission. Since then, more than 30 trees across the city have been designated as Piedmont’s “Heritage Trees.” The intent of the program is to recognize noteworthy and distinctive trees located in Piedmont’s parks and open spaces, encourage residents to visit those spaces, and promote the study and appreciation of nature. Walker and Park Commissioner Jack Fischrup told the group that the commission has been working for several years to install signs marking the existing Heritage Trees. The cost of the markers has now been approved and included in the City’s budget. The signs are expected to be installed by Arbor Day in April. Members of the Wednesday walking group have played a role in the program’s history. In 2023 the walkers nominated the mulberry trees in front of the Piedmont Play School at Hampton Park as a Heritage Tree candidate. With the enthusiastic help of the school’s young students— who also submitted the nomination—the trees won designation. The following year the walkers had another success when a Park’s Cherry Walk and Tea House area. At the bottom of the steps the walkers encountered several more Heritage Trees. Japanese maples added delicate color and form to the landscape, and nearby stood a group of Akebono cherry trees. In front of Community Hall, the walkers paused at a Yulan magnolia, known for its striking white blossoms in the spring. Continuing past Community Hall, the group stopped beside a large, twisting Coast live oak that has served as a backdrop for countless family photos over the decades. It is also a Heritage Tree and provided a good setting for the walkers’ group photograph. Nearby, behind the Exedra’s tot lot, the walkers saw another grouping of Coast live oaks. From there the group climbed Highland Avenue to Vista Avenue and City Hall, where a group of Evergreen dogwoods stands at the entrance. The walkers then continued down Vista and Bonita Avenues, passing the city’s new pool. The group will have an opportunity to visit the facility on March 25 during a tour with Recreation Director Chelle Putzer. At the Recreation Center on Hillside Avenue the walkers paused to admire a palm tree standing to the left of the building. The tree was a 2023 Heritage Tree winner nominated by Recreation staff and Hillside Preschool students. Known as a Canary Island date palm, the species is popular because its trunk stays relatively narrow while the canopy forms a symmetrical crown. The group then continued up Hillside Avenue to Blair Avenue Walter Blair grove of eucalyptus trees in lower Piedmont Park received Heritage Tree status. Their submission last year did not make the podium, but 2026 brings another opportunity. Nominations are due March 20, and the winners will be announced before Arbor Day on April 23. The group decided to revisit some past winners and begin thinking about what tree they might nominate this year. The first Heritage Trees were close at hand. Surrounding the Exedra Plaza is a grove of ten Highland poplars that have been designated Heritage Trees. From there the walkers headed up to the Community Hall parking lot to admire a community favorite that is not covered with lights this time of year. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, March 11, 2026 Walking on Wednesday By Dick Carter Forty-five walkers and four K-9 companions gathered at the Exedra last Wednesday morning for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays outing. The group set out to revisit several of Piedmont’s parks and take a closer look at some of the city’s Heritage Trees. The Piedmont Heritage Tree Program was created in 2018 by the City Council based on a recommendation from the Park Commission. Since then, more than 30 trees across the city have been designated as Piedmont’s “Heritage Trees.” The intent of the program is to recognize noteworthy and distinctive trees located in Piedmont’s parks and open spaces, encourage residents to visit those spaces, and promote the study and appreciation of nature. Walker and Park Commissioner Jack Fischrup told the group that the commission has been working for several years to install signs marking the existing Heritage Trees. The cost of the markers has now been approved and included in the City’s budget. The signs are expected to be installed by Arbor Day in April. Members of the Wednesday walking group have played a role in the program’s history. In 2023 the walkers nominated the mulberry trees in front of the Piedmont Play School at Hampton Park as a Heritage Tree candidate. With the enthusiastic help of the school’s young students— who also submitted the nomination—the trees won designation. The following year the walkers had another success when a Wednesday Walkers Explore Piedmont’s Heritage Trees Park’s Cherry Walk and Tea House area. At the bottom of the steps the walkers encountered several more Heritage Trees. Japanese maples added delicate color and form to the landscape, and nearby stood a group of Akebono cherry trees. In front of Community Hall, the walkers paused at a Yulan magnolia, known for its striking white blossoms in the spring. Continuing past Community Hall, the group stopped beside a large, twisting Coast live oak that has served as a backdrop for countless family photos over the decades. It is also a Heritage Tree and provided a good setting for the walkers’ group photograph. Nearby, behind the Exedra’s tot lot, the walkers saw another grouping of Coast live oaks. From there the group climbed Highland Avenue to Vista Avenue and City Hall, where a group of Evergreen dogwoods stands at the entrance. The walkers then continued down Vista and Bonita Avenues, passing the city’s new pool. The group will have an opportunity to visit the facility on March 25 during a tour with Recreation Director Chelle Putzer. At the Recreation Center on Hillside Avenue the walkers paused to admire a palm tree standing to the left of the building. The tree was a 2023 Heritage Tree winner nominated by Recreation staff and Hillside Preschool students. Known as a Canary Island date palm, the species is popular because its trunk stays relatively narrow while the canopy forms a symmetrical crown. The group then continued up Hillside Avenue to Blair Avenue Walter Blair grove of eucalyptus trees in lower Piedmont Park received Heritage Tree status. Their submission last year did not make the podium, but 2026 brings another opportunity. Nominations are due March 20, and the winners will be announced before Arbor Day on April 23. The group decided to revisit some past winners and begin thinking about what tree they might nominate this year. The first Heritage Trees were close at hand. Surrounding the Exedra Plaza is a grove of ten Highland poplars that have been designated Heritage Trees. From there the walkers headed up to the Community Hall parking lot to admire a community favorite that is not covered with lights this time of year. The Coast Redwood that serves as Piedmont’s holiday tree is also a Heritage Tree. The group then made its way up and down the Highland-Guilford Steps, a project completed by the City in 2023 with support from the Piedmont Beautification Foundation. The steps create a welcoming entrance to Piedmont Map of route and entered Dracena Park. Commissioner Fischrup guided the walkers to see several more Heritage Trees: another mature Coast live oak, a California buckeye, a native bigleaf maple, and a grove of six dawn redwoods located toward the back of the park on the site of Walter Blair’s 1850s quarry. Along the park’s upper path the walkers stopped at Storyteller Bridge, which crosses the park’s ravine. Max Becker shared how his younger brother rebuilt the bridge as an Eagle Scout project with help from family members, the City, and community volunteers. The group emerged from the park on Park Way and walked down to the bend where the street becomes Monticello Avenue. Along the way Sherry Jacobs joked that Park Way might more accurately be called Magnolia Avenue because of the many magnolia trees lining the street— even though Magnolia Avenue itself has none. A hidden path at the end of Park Way led the walkers back into Dracena Park to see the grove of dawn redwoods more closely. These remarkable trees once grew widely in California about one million years ago and were long believed extinct until they were rediscovered in central China in 1948. Today they are one of three living redwood species, along with the Coast Redwood and the Giant Sequoia. From the park’s play area the group looked down toward a stand of Southern magnolias with dramatic exposed roots—trees the walkers themselves nominated last year as a Heritage Tree candidate. The walkers then climbed the stairs near the play area to El Cerrito Avenue and continued up to Blair Avenue. Along the way it was noted that Walter Blair and his brother introduced eucalyptus trees to the Piedmont area in the late 19th century. The trees were planted as a boundary between what is now Mountain View Cemetery and Piedmont and were once known locally as “Blair’s Gum Trees.” They were removed in 1936 when the road was widened. The group had hoped to see several more Heritage Trees on streets to the south, but the morning had passed quickly. It was time to return to the Exedra via Carmel, Oakland, and Highland Avenues. The walkers had seen a number of Piedmont’s beautiful and historic trees—and there were more waiting to be discovered on future walks. They will also have to decide which tree deserves the group’s nomination for the 2026 Heritage Tree. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 AM. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with is required. Those interested should go to https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu to register or call at (510) 420-3070 for more information. On January 31, 2026, wine lovers gathered in downtown San Jose for the Festival of Undiscovered Grapes, an immersive wine-tasting celebration highlighting the world’s rare and lesser-known grape varieties. The event drew local residents and visitors eager to explore beyond familiar varietals like Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, and Pinot Noir. Instead, guests sipped wines made from “underdog” grapes — including Semillon, Teroldego, Tannant, Bourbolenc, Cinsault, and Trousseau — representing more than 110 unique winegrape varieties grown in California. With dozens of wineries pouring their distinctive selections, attendees wandered the room sampling bold reds, aromatic whites, and intriguing blends that many had never encountered before. Wine producers from across the state were on hand to share stories of their vineyards and the heritage of these lesser-known grapes, offering insight into the diversity of California’s wine landscape. Participants could choose between general admission and VIP tickets. VIP guests enjoyed early access, a pre-tasting discussion focused on Lodi wine varietals with experts, a commemorative wine glass, and complimentary delivery of bottles ordered at the event. General admission ticket holders joined the tasting after the VIP session and had the option to have their wine purchases delivered for a flat fee. A food vendor on site offered small bites and snacks to pair with the wines, creating a festive atmosphere throughout the afternoon. Conversations flowed as easily as the pours, with many oenophiles excited to discover new favorites and broaden their palates. Organizers said the festival aimed not just to entertain but to educate, spotlighting vinicultural diversity and supporting small producers whose bottles might otherwise go unnoticed. For many attendees, the event succeeded in turning curiosity into appreciation, underscoring that California’s wine story extends far beyond its most popular grapes. On January 31, 2026, wine lovers gathered in downtown San Jose for the Festival of Undiscovered Grapes, an immersive wine-tasting celebration highlighting the world’s rare and lesser-known grape varieties. With dozens of wineries pouring their distinctive selections, attendees wandered the room sampling bold reds, aromatic whites, and intriguing blends that many had never encountered before. Wine producers from across the state were on hand to share stories of their vineyards and the heritage of these lesser-known grapes, offering insight into the diversity of California’s wine landscape. Participants could choose between general admission and VIP tickets. VIP guests enjoyed early access, a pre-tasting discussion focused on Lodi wine varietals with experts, a commemorative wine glass, and complimentary delivery of bottles ordered at the event. General admission ticket holders joined the tasting after the VIP session and had the option to have their wine purchases delivered for a flat fee. A food vendor on site offered small bites and snacks to pair with the wines, creating a festive atmosphere throughout the afternoon. Conversations flowed as easily as the pours, with many oenophiles excited to discover new favorites and broaden their palates. For many attendees, the event succeeded in turning curiosity into appreciation, underscoring that California’s wine story extends far beyond its most popular grapes. The following wines were the standouts of the huge tasting. They are the cream of the crop and are worth searching out. WHITE WINES • 2024 Tansy Fiano, $36 This interesting grape is originally from the Taurasi region in southern Italy. The wine opens to fine, dusty, mineral aromas, followed by sweet citrus, lemon peel and apricot. This lean-bodied white ends with zippy acidity and a touch of zesty spice. Very foodfriendly it would go with seafood of any kind. In the mouth there are easy layers of apple, stone fruit and crushed stone that add depth and character. The finish is clean and satisfying. Beautiful wine! • 2024 Vigo Picpoul Blanc, $45 Picpoul, a minor grape from the south of France, seems to be gaining popularity in California. The name in French means “lipstinger” and it is known for its bracing acidity. This version from Paso Robles balances out that acidity with abundant melon, apple and pear fruit. It has aromas of lime zest and slate, is medium bodied and has a smooth, clean finish. Perfect aperitif. • 2024 Andis Semillon Bill Dillian Vineyard, $25 Coming from a 45-year-old vineyard in the Shenandoah Valley this grape is predominantly grown in southwest France and Australia. It is grassy and intense, with apple, straw, vanilla and wax. The palate follows with a stream of juicy acidity that flows through the fruit. The mouthfeel is weighty and round with a long lingering finish. The world needs a little less Sauvignon Blanc and a little more Semillon. • 2024 Perlegos Assyrtiko, $29 Usually, you must go to Santorini to taste this wine but leave it to the Greek-owned Perlegos winery in Lodi to import Greece’s best white grape and give it the old California try. It is succulent and fleshy, with brine, apple, pear and vanilla wafer aromas. It is complex and impressively layered, with texture and flavor in profusion. A great foodfriendly wine it would go with a wide range of meals from fish to chicken to cheese. The Assyrtiko grape is Greece’s finest white. RED WINES • 2023 Giornata Aglianico, $40 Aglianico is the most noble grape from southern Italy and is used to make sturdy, dense, longaged reds. This version from Paso Robles Giornata Winery is a gentle giant with dark fruit, earth, leather and warm spice. I could imagine lamb chops on the grill as a delicious food match. The wine ends with firm tannins, but the effect is not bitter because plenty of dark fruit remains throughout. • 2018 Kinetic Tinto Moderno, $15 (Best Value) This is a field blend of five Portuguese varietals Tinta Roritz, Touriga Nacional, Touriga Francesca, Souzao and Alvarelhao. It is a light and fruity wine with lots of finesse and style. Redolent of blueberries and red currants it is fresh and vibrant on the palate with a touch of acid on the finish. A remarkable value, this wine should be drunk now. Kinetic Cellars red blend was the best value of the tasting. • 2019 Post & Vine Carignane Contra Costa County, $24 This wine comes from one of the greatest, most overlooked vineyard areas in California. Tucked away in Contra Costa County near the town of Oakley are some sandy loam vineyards that are home of gnarly, century-old vines of Carignane and Mourvedre producing wines of great character. The wine is medium ruby in color and prettily perfumed, with fresh plum and blueberry fruit with notes of earth and a streak of graphite. The palate offers bright, fresh fruit character with loads of uplift and a long, floral-laced finish. Beautiful stuff to drink over the next 7-8 years. The Fiano grape from Italy shines in this Russian River wine. • 2023 Intercostal Wines Pinotage Bianco $35 This could be the rarest wine of all at the Festival of Undiscovered Grapes. As far as I know Lodi’s Intercoastal is the only winery to make a white version of this famous South African grape anywhere. The nose has aromas of honeysuckle, melon and citrus. It is beautiful, velvety, beefy, complex and well-balanced. The tannins are present but not overpowering with layers of cassis, raspberries, and earth. It is round and full in the mouth with a savory complex finish. This example from the El Dorado Hills AVA is ripe, dense and personable, with some nuances of anise, roast beef and blackberries. This is an expressive Tannat that shows fine structure and even better concentration. This big blockbuster of a wine begs for a grilled ribeye steak. • 2024 Marchelle Cinsault Bechtold Vineyard, $54 Cinsault is one of the main blending grapes used in the south of France but is seldom bottled on its own there. I am glad to see some American wineries are starting to correct that as it is delightful on its own. Sort of like a cross between Pinot Noir and Grenache the bouquet reveals pure cherry fruit, with currants and pomegranate. It is light and vibrant on the palate; fairly simple but juicy, refreshing and satisfying. • 2022 Comunita Schioppettino, $55 What a fun discovery – another grape I have not only never tasted but never even heard of! The winemaker explained that it originally comes from the Friuli region of northern Italy with these grapes coming from a small vineyard in the Russian River Valley. The wine opens to a rustic bouquet of tart cherries, smoke, tar and earth. The bouquet is totally offbeat, but it is also bursting with authentic personality. The mouthfeel is bright, crisp and refreshing. Really interesting wine worth seeking out. • 2023 Alta Colina “Sun Worshipper”, $68 A blend of 61% Mouvedre and 30% Syrah from Paso Robles the Sun Worshipper is a blockbuster of juicy goodness. Aromatically, it leads with lashings of black fruits and berries, exotic spices and almost no hint of oak. In the mouth, the wine is a mirror image, with the added experience of fine tannins. This lovely wine, opulent yet nimble with great balance, finishes long and savory. ]• 2019 Anaya Nebbiolo, $48 Nebbiolo is famously hard to grow anywhere except in its homeland of Northern Italy so it is rarely attempted in California. This bottling from Lodi has some of the classic roses and tar nose the grape is known for. It delivers flavors of cherries, herbs and cranberries in the medium bodied style. The finish combines a bright, high-toned energy with assertive yet refined tannins and a lovely perfume. • 2024 Camin Dreams Mencia, $40 Sourced from a vineyard in San Benito County this rare grape from the north of Spain is rarely seen in the US. It produces a light-bodied, finesse style wine similar to Pinot Noir. Pale in color it has a young, fruit-driven nose with some floral notes, with an herbal touch and nice cherry fruit. The palate is juicy and tender, with very fine tannins, very clean and precise. The perfect wine to go with any preparation of salmon. • 2023 Trail Marker Trousseau Petites Joies, $28 Perhaps the lightest in color of all red wines, Trousseau originally from the Jura region of France, looks like a Tavel rose. This bottling from the Russian River Valley has lots of sediment showing it was made naturally and unfiltered. The wine is clean and bright, with a perfumed nose with notes of violets and a light bodied palate with subtle fine tannins. There’s balance and a certain earthiness. Delicious now it should be drunk in the next one to two years. • 2024 Derby Counoise, $46 Paso Robles’ Derby Winery has taken a grape that seldom escapes the blending bench in France and given it a star turn. It gives up lively cherry, violets, dried spices and a kiss of earth to go with the medium-bodied, supple and lively feel on the palate. Eminently quaffable this is a beautiful example of the variety to drink over the next 3-4 years.

Haku warns Chihiro to avoid the witch, but she is told she must serve the malevolent hag in order to return her parents to their original forms. And so begins Chihiro’s extraordinary journey through the park, meeting a host of demons and strange creatures. There are dragons, frogmen, a giant and very cranky baby, a spidery furnace stoker and other inhabitants that take her breath away. And so, this once fearful, contrary girl must face the museum-like, harrowing, spirit-filled place and learn to be brave for the sake of herself and her parents. Ultimately, it is her transformation that is at the center of Spirited Away. The animation, as expected, is dazzling, rich and lush and soft, each frame a hand drawn work of art. Of course, the story is unusual, steeped in Japanese mythology, and may be more appealing to young girls; however, boys will also enjoy the spectrum of mysterious spirits, especially Yubaba. articles.text: Early Bird Registration now open Piedmont Food Fest is turning five this year! The Bay Area’s most vibrant multicultural festival returns to Piedmont Park on Saturday, April 25, from 11 a.m. - 4 p.m. Since launching in 2022, this volunteer-run event has become a community tradition of building shared experiences through food, drink, music, and arts. By connecting over 2000 attendees with 50 local businesses and community organizations, Piedmont Food Fest sets the stage for a day full of new experiences and memories for visitors of all ages. With its wide variety of sights, sounds, and tastes, Piedmont Food Fest has evolved into an event for the greater Bay Area, with many guests visiting from San Francisco, Marin, Fremont, and Danville. Piedmont residents often seize the opportunity to invite friends and family to spend the day together at the festival. Visit www.piedmontfoodfest. org to sign up for event updates as well as check out Early Bird specials for discounted drink packages & KidZone bracelets through March. This event is free to the public, and all are encouraged to invite friends and family to enjoy this day together. This year, Piedmont Food Fest will feature: • Food and dessert vendors: Casablanca Moroccan & Mediterranean, Aburaya Japanese Fried Chicken, Momolicious, BBtea, Hint of Desi, Cousins Maine Lobster, Aloha Aria’s Shave Ice, Swahili Spot, Arthur Mac’s, Lola’s Spanish Cuisine, Sunrise Deli, Bonito Poke, Lizetta’s Southern Soul Food, Crazy Empanadas, Pintoh Thai, and 3 Brothers Kitchen. • Local breweries and wineries: Oakland United, Farmstead Wines, P. Herrell Winery, and Covenant Wines – plus a rotating sangria and frosé station. • Live performances: Wilbert McAlister’s Cowboy and His Sometimes Blues Band, DJ HeyLove, the Purple Silk Youth Orchestra, Beloved Aerial Arts, Piedmont Middle School, Han Martial Arts, and a special performance by the Cal Band! • The KidZone: features ten carnival booths, a kid-favorite sno-cone station, and a multicultural crafts table. • Community groups & local retailers including PHS for Alameda Food Bank, No Immigrant No Spice, Immedium Books, Porschia’s Henna Tattoos, and Heather’s Face Painting. The installation and expansion of cameras in Oakland, San Leandro, Emeryville and other cities has also helped the region address vehicle theft. “The camera alerts our officers receive enable them to quickly identify whether those vehicles are coming in or out of our city,” Chief Shavies added. “And even in those that we don’t recover, we’re able to contact Oakland and let them know that they have one coming.” Through the continued use of ALPR cameras, Chief Shavies said residents’ privacy remains an important priority. The department works with Flock Safety to ensure the system complies with state requirements and community expectations. “I think it’s important that we feel the same concerns, and we have certain guardrails in place that will ensure that our entire community, and those that travel through, their privacy is respected,” said Chief Shavies. PPD continues to maintain direct authority over who is granted access to the city network. “Not only will we, but Flock Safety also will not share any of our data with anyone for any immigration reasons, or for any reproductive care reasons,” he said. In 2025, PPD continued its community outreach programs, including Cop on the Block and Coffee, Cars, and Cops. Youth engagement also continued through the department’s partnership with the Piedmont Unified School District for campus safety planning, drills and day-to-day coordination. “I think that in seeing me in the community, it’s not just about being visible, it’s also about listening and understanding the needs, the wants, and the desires of our community,” he said. The year 2026 will be PPD’s first full year under Chief Shavies. His priorities include increasing staffing and dispatch operations, continuing investments in training, maintaining proactive policing strategies and strengthening internal systems and accountability. “I want us to be one of the top police departments in the region in the way that we are addressing and reducing crime, the way that we’re responding to the members of our community, and in a way that we’re trained,” said Chief Shavies.
